page_title: GNN Training: Sampling Strategies and Batch Normalization
summary: This lecture page details methods to improve the computational efficiency and stability of training Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on large graphs. It contrasts three primary sampling strategies—node-wise (GraphSAGE), layer-wise (FastGCN), and subgraph-based (ClusterGCN, GraphSAINT)—highlighting their trade-offs regarding memory usage, redundancy, and structural preservation. Additionally, it explains the role of Batch Normalization (BN) in stabilizing forward propagation, controlling covariate shift, and enabling higher learning rates through regularization.

concepts.evidence: Node sampling: Randomly select a subset of target nodes and then work back through the network adding a subset of the nodes in the receptive field at each stage.
Layer sampling samples the receptive field in each layer independently. This addresses the node increase in node sampling as we pass back through the graph.
Subgraph sampling: Randomly draws subgraphs or divide the original graph into subgraphs. These are trained as independent data samples.
Computational Efficiency: Node sampling reduces the computational cost by training on a subset of nodes rather than the entire graph.
Memory Efficiency: It allows for more efficient memory usage, especially when dealing with graphs with a large number of nodes.
Scalability: It allows GNNs to scale to very large graphs by breaking them down into manageable pieces.
Local structure disruption: It may disrupt the links connecting neighboring nodes between two consecutive layers due to the random independent sampling in each layer.
Redundant computations: The recursive nature of node-wise sampling brings in redundancy for calculating embeddings.
Information Loss: Sampling may result in information loss, as the model is trained on a subset of the graph instead of the entire structure.
Sampling Bias: The sampling process may introduce biases, especially if certain parts of the graph are consistently under-sampled.
Limited Global Information: Sampling might limit the model's ability to capture global graph properties, which could be crucial for certain tasks.
LADIES (Zou et al., 2019): layer-dependent importance sampling
